strengths: Introduces a promptable 3D part segmentation model trained natively on large-scale 3D data, addressing key limitations of 2D-lifted methods such as surface-only understanding and limited controllability.
Proposes a scalable triplane-based dual-branch encoder and SAM-style prompt-guided decoder, enabling both interactive segmentation and automatic 'Segment Every Part' decomposition.
Develops a model-in-the-loop data curation pipeline that scales supervision to about 500k shapes and over 5M parts, with ablations showing clear benefits from native and augmented data.

Reports strong empirical results: large gains over Point-SAM in interactive segmentation and state-of-the-art performance against multiple baselines in automatic segmentation, including on AI-generated meshes.
Provides useful ablation studies, complexity analysis, and downstream applications such as interior part editing and amodal segmentation, supporting the practical value of the model.
weaknesses: The architecture largely combines existing components (PartField triplane encoder, SAM-style decoder, prompt simulation), so the conceptual novelty is moderate despite strong engineering and scaling.

The 'native 3D supervision' claim is partially qualified: the frozen PartField branch and PartField-generated pseudo-labels in the model-in-the-loop pipeline still inject 2D SAM-derived priors into training.

Automatic segmentation evaluation raises fairness concerns: mesh connectivity is disabled for PartField but not for SAMesh, and with connectivity PartField's gap to PartSAM narrows substantially (e.g., 79.2 vs. 81.3 on PartObjaverse-Tiny in the appendix).

Quantitative evaluation is limited to two main datasets, interactive segmentation is compared only to Point-SAM, and there are no error bars or statistical significance tests; semantic labels are also not predicted.
Reproducibility is not fully demonstrated at submission time: code/model are only promised, dataset curation depends on online assets, and key model-in-the-loop filtering thresholds are hand-tuned.
The manuscript has minor presentation issues, including several typos and reference/formatting inconsistencies.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: open-world 3D part segmentation with promptable, feed-forward inference.
Proposes a SAM-style promptable decoder for 3D part segmentation, enabling both interactive segmentation and an automatic 'Segment Every Part' mode.
Attempts a large-scale 3D data curation pipeline, scaling to roughly 500k shapes and 5M part annotations if the labels are reliable.
The dual-branch triplane encoder is a reasonable architectural idea for combining 2D foundation-model priors with native 3D fine-tuning.
Provides extensive experiments, including interactive segmentation, automatic segmentation, ablations, application examples, and a complexity analysis.
Reports strong quantitative improvements on the chosen benchmarks and shows convincing qualitative results on diverse shapes.
Ablation studies examine both encoder design and training-data scale, which helps clarify the contribution of each component.
The paper is generally well organized at a high level and the promised code/model release would aid future research.
weaknesses: The central 'native 3D' and 'first' claims are overstated: the encoder is initialized from PartField, one branch is frozen to preserve SAM-distilled 2D priors, and the data pipeline uses PartField pseudo-labels. The method therefore still depends heavily on the 2D-lifting paradigm it claims to avoid.

Potential train-test overlap/contamination is not addressed: training uses Objaverse and PartNet/ABO, while evaluation uses PartObjaverse-Tiny and PartNetE. The paper does not specify explicit splits or exclusion of evaluation shapes, making the reported gains difficult to trust.

The data supervision is of uncertain quality. The 'model-in-the-loop' annotations are generated by PartField and filtered by PartSAM itself, which may amplify existing biases rather than produce reliable native 3D ground truth. No human verification or label-noise analysis is provided.

The evaluation protocol is not fully fair or standard. Interactive segmentation is compared only against Point-SAM, while automatic segmentation evaluates baselines under modified settings (e.g., PartField without mesh connectivity, SAMesh with connectivity) and uses best-of-multiple candidate masks for baselines.

The claimed advantage in capturing interior 3D structure is demonstrated mainly qualitatively. There is no quantitative benchmark for interior or amodal part segmentation to substantiate this as a core contribution.

The technical novelty is limited. The decoder is a fairly direct adaptation of SAM's mask decoder to point clouds, and the encoder is largely inherited from PartField; the dual-branch frozen/fine-tuned design is a straightforward combination rather than a fundamentally new formulation.

Reproducibility is weak. Code, model, and curated data are not yet available, and key details of the data pipeline, pseudo-label filtering, de-duplication, and train/test split are missing. Training on 8 H20 GPUs with 500k shapes is also difficult to reproduce.

Important implementation details are underspecified, including prompt encoding, triplane feature sampling, dual-branch fusion, loss weighting, and how automatic mask selection thresholds are tuned without using test labels.
Writing quality is poor, with numerous typos, broken sentences, malformed references, and inconsistent notation. This hampers clarity and makes the claims harder to evaluate.

Comparisons are narrow. The paper omits comparisons to several recent open-world 3D part segmentation methods on interactive tasks and does not evaluate text-conditioned or semantic part segmentation, despite discussing open-world applicability.
The complexity analysis reports only inference time and parameter count; training cost, memory scaling, and behavior as data/model scale increase are not analyzed, weakening the 'scalable' claim.
The model still cannot produce semantic labels for parts, which limits its practical utility for downstream tasks where category-aware part labels are needed.

strengths: Introduces a promptable 3D part segmentation model trained on large-scale native 3D shape-part pairs, a clear step beyond 2D-lifting and clustering-based approaches.

Triplane dual-branch encoder design effectively combines a frozen PartField branch to retain 2D/SAM priors with a learnable native-3D branch, and the prompt-guided decoder enables flexible interactive and automatic segmentation.
Scales supervision to 500k shapes and more than 5 million parts via a model-in-the-loop annotation pipeline, which is a substantial data contribution.
Achieves strong empirical results: large gains over Point-SAM in interactive segmentation and over SAMesh, SAMPart3D, and PartField in automatic segmentation on multiple benchmarks.
Ablation studies support the importance of the dual-branch encoder and large-scale curated data; complexity analysis shows feed-forward efficiency compared with per-shape optimization methods.
weaknesses: Evaluation fairness for automatic segmentation is not fully resolved: disabling mesh connectivity for PartField puts it at a disadvantage, while PartSAM can also use connectivity and PartField with connectivity/training reaches 79.2 on PartObjaverse-Tiny, higher than the main PartSAM result of 69.5. The main table should include both connectivity settings transparently.

The data annotation pipeline is partially circular: PartField pseudo-labels are filtered by PartSAM itself, which may introduce self-training bias. The paper lacks independent quantitative validation of pseudo-label accuracy.

The claim of being trained natively on 3D data is weakened by initializing and freezing one encoder branch from PartField, which itself was trained with SAM-derived 2D supervision; the contribution is better described as hybrid native-3D training rather than fully native 3D supervision.

Reproducibility is limited at review time: code/model are not yet released, dataset construction details are incomplete, and some training/evaluation protocols rely on external components with unspecified versions or configurations.

Method and experimental details are sometimes underspecified, such as negative prompt handling, upsampling/interpolation, and exact baseline training/evaluation protocols. The manuscript also contains several typographical and notation errors (e.g., 'duan-branch').
The model does not produce semantic part labels, which limits usefulness for downstream tasks requiring categories; the paper acknowledges this but does not evaluate it.
Some baselines are evaluated under settings that may not reflect their best performance, and the paper does not fully disentangle gains from architecture, data scale, and promptable training.

strengths: Introduces a promptable 3D part segmentation model trained on large-scale native 3D annotations, with a SAM-like encoder-decoder and a dual-branch triplane encoder that combines a frozen 2D-prior branch with a learnable 3D-native branch.
Proposes a model-in-the-loop data curation pipeline that scales supervision to 500k shapes and over 5M shape-part pairs, addressing the scarcity of native 3D part labels.

Reports strong empirical gains over Point-SAM, SAMPart3D, SAMesh, PartField, and other baselines on interactive and automatic part segmentation, with additional qualitative results on AI-generated meshes and interior part segmentation.

Includes useful ablations on architecture and training data, a scaling curve, complexity analysis, cross-shape consistency analysis, and demonstrations of downstream applications such as interior part editing and amodal part segmentation.
The automatic 'Segment Every Part' mode is a practical and promising extension of the interactive promptable segmentation framework.
weaknesses: Potential training/evaluation data leakage is not adequately addressed. The method trains on Objaverse(-XL), PartNet, and ABO, while evaluation uses PartObjaverse-Tiny and PartNetE, which are likely derived from overlapping sources. No explicit train/test separation or exclusion of benchmark shapes is described, which threatens the validity of the headline quantitative results.

The claim of being trained 'natively on large-scale 3D data' is overstated. The encoder is initialized from PartField, which is trained with 2D SAM-derived supervision, and the second-stage pseudo-labels are generated by PartField. Thus the model still depends heavily on 2D foundation-model priors and PartField outputs, rather than being purely native 3D supervision.

Evaluation fairness and reproducibility are insufficiently clear. Interactive segmentation is compared only against Point-SAM; automatic segmentation baselines are evaluated under different settings (e.g., connectivity disabled only for PartField, SAMesh using original connectivity), and the use of 'best' multi-scale scores and unclear mask-matching/label-assignment protocols could affect comparisons. Code, data, and exact train/test splits are not clearly released or specified.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the architecture combines existing components such as PartField's triplane representation, a SAM-style decoder, PVCNN, connected-component supervision, and PartField-generated pseudo-labels. The main contribution is a large-scale system/data integration rather than a fundamentally new segmentation method.

The pseudo-labeling pipeline is potentially circular: PartSAM is pretrained on PartField outputs and then used to filter PartField-generated pseudo-labels, which may reinforce PartField biases and inflate apparent agreement.

Some design choices and evaluation details remain under-specified, including how NMS thresholds are selected for automatic segmentation, how masks are matched to instance-level ground truth, and how much the reported gains depend on hyperparameter tuning.

strengths: Targets an important and challenging problem: open-world, promptable 3D part segmentation with a feed-forward model.
The proposed large-scale data curation pipeline is ambitious, scaling to 500k shapes and over 5M part annotations, with a scaling curve suggesting continued gains with more data.

The architecture is reasonably designed, combining triplane feature fields, a dual-branch encoder, and a SAM-style prompt-guided decoder; it enables interactive and automatic segmentation in a single framework.
Empirical results on PartObjaverse-Tiny and PartNet-E show large improvements over Point-SAM for interactive segmentation and over several automatic baselines.
The paper includes useful ablations on architecture and training data, plus applications such as interior part editing, amodal segmentation, cross-shape consistency, and complexity analysis.
Qualitative examples on AI-generated and artist-created meshes are compelling and illustrate capabilities such as segmenting occluded/interior structures.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited and somewhat oversold: the encoder is initialized from PartField, the frozen branch preserves SAM-derived 2D priors, the triplet contrastive loss is taken from PartField, and the decoder closely follows SAM. The 'first native 3D' framing is weakened by this heavy reliance on prior 2D/SAM-lifted supervision.

The automatic segmentation evaluation appears unfair or at least inconsistent. PartField is crippled by disabling mesh connectivity and using K-Means, while SAMesh is evaluated with its connectivity-based pipeline. Table 4 shows PartField with connectivity and training reaches 79.2 IoU, close to PartSAM's 81.3 with connectivity, so the headline 69.5 vs 51.5 margin is misleading.

The model-in-the-loop annotation pipeline is circular: PartField pseudo-labels are filtered by PartSAM, which was itself pretrained on PartField-derived priors. This may propagate existing biases, and no human verification or independent quality audit is provided.

Interactive segmentation is compared only with Point-SAM. Other promptable/interactive 3D segmentation approaches or human-in-the-loop baselines are absent, making the generality of the interactive claims uncertain.

Evaluation is narrow and lacks statistical rigor: main results are single mean-IoU numbers on two datasets, with no error bars, significance tests, or per-category breakdowns. Interior/amodal claims are supported mainly qualitatively, without quantitative benchmarks.

Reproducibility is insufficient: no code or dataset release is described in the manuscript, and the data curation, filtering thresholds, and model-in-the-loop acceptance rules are complex and not fully specified. Training requires substantial resources (8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs, 250k iterations), which limits reproducibility.

The automatic 'Segment Every Part' pipeline depends on FPS prompt density, NMS thresholds, and predicted IoU selection. Robustness to these hyperparameters and failure modes is not adequately evaluated.

Several technical/clarity issues remain: inconsistent Point-SAM numbers between Table 1 and Table 3, some typographical/grammatical errors, and claims such as 'decisive step toward foundation models' are stronger than the evidence supports.

strengths: Introduces PartSAM, the first promptable 3D part segmentation model trained natively on large-scale 3D data, with a clear contribution beyond 2D-lifting approaches.
The dual-branch triplane encoder is a sensible and scalable design: it preserves SAM/PartField priors in a frozen branch while adapting a learnable branch to native 3D supervision.
The model-in-the-loop data curation pipeline is a substantial engineering contribution, scaling to ~500k shapes and >5M shape-part pairs, with a demonstrated scaling curve.
Strong empirical results: PartSAM outperforms state-of-the-art methods by large margins on interactive and automatic part segmentation across PartObjaverse-Tiny, PartNetE, and 3DCoMPaT++.
Thorough experimental analysis, including ablations on encoder design, pre-trained weights, training data, mesh connectivity, complexity, cross-shape consistency, and failure cases.
Supports useful downstream applications such as interior part editing and amodal part segmentation, and the automatic 'Segment Every Part' mode is practically valuable.
weaknesses: The model-in-the-loop annotation pipeline depends on PartField pseudo-labels, which may propagate PartField's clustering biases and limit the diversity/quality of supervision.
The data curation is fully automated and lacks human verification; the authors acknowledge remaining imperfect labels and long-tail part types, which could affect reliability.
The evaluation reports best scores over multiple candidate masks/scales for some baselines and ours, which can obscure per-granularity performance and may favor methods with more candidate masks.
PartSAM remains class-agnostic and cannot assign semantic labels to masks, limiting direct use in downstream tasks requiring semantic part understanding.
Interactive segmentation is mainly compared against Point-SAM; adding more promptable or interactive 3D segmentation baselines would further strengthen the claims.
Quantitative evaluation on real-world scanned data is relatively limited, with some real-scan results only qualitative or shown as failure cases.
There are minor clarity issues in the manuscript (e.g., awkward phrasing around the dual-branch encoder description and a few typographical/grammatical slips).
